title: Meeting Point

source.name: Original exercise; classic technique (lowest common ancestor, binary lifting)

statement:
A company hierarchy is a rooted tree with employee `1` at the top. Employee `v` (for `v` from `2` to `n`) reports directly to employee `p[v]`, and `p[v] < v`. For two employees, their **meeting point** is the lowest employee who is an ancestor of both (an employee counts as their own ancestor).

**Input.** First line: `n` and `q`. Second line: `p[2], p[3], ..., p[n]`. Then `q` lines `u v`.

**Output.** For every query, the meeting point of `u` and `v`, one per line.
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 20000, 1 ≤ q ≤ 20000 in this browser version (the idea scales to 2·10^5)
hints: Climbing one parent at a time costs O(depth) per query, which is O(n) on a path.
Precompute up[k][v], the 2^k-th ancestor of v. Then any number of steps up is a sum of powers of two, i.e. O(log n) jumps.

First lift the deeper vertex to the same depth. If they are equal you are done. Otherwise, for k from high to low, jump both while their 2^k-th ancestors differ; the answer is the parent of where you stop.
editorial: Binary lifting stores `up[k][v]`, the `2^k`-th ancestor of `v`, computed by `up[k][v] = up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]`, in `O(n log n)` time and memory. To answer a query, first lift the deeper vertex by the depth difference, one set bit at a time, so both vertices are at the same depth. If they now coincide that vertex is the answer. Otherwise their ancestors coincide from the LCA upwards and differ below it, so jumping from the highest power of two downwards, only when the ancestors differ, lands both vertices just below the LCA, and the answer is their parent. Each query is `O(log n)`. Because `p[v] < v`, depths can be computed in input order with no search. The naive method is `O(depth)` per query and fails on a path of `10^5` vertices.

starter.python:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, q = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
# parents p[2..n] are data[2:1 + n]; the q queries follow

solutions.python:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, q = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
LOG = max(1, n.bit_length())
up = [[1] * (n + 1) for _ in range(LOG)]     # up[k][v] = the 2^k-th ancestor of v (the root points to itself)
depth = [0] * (n + 1)
for v in range(2, n + 1):
    up[0][v] = int(data[v])
    depth[v] = depth[up[0][v]] + 1           # parents have smaller numbers, so they are ready
for k in range(1, LOG):
    for v in range(1, n + 1):
        up[k][v] = up[k - 1][up[k - 1][v]]
out = []
pos = n + 1
for _ in range(q):
    u, v = int(data[pos]), int(data[pos + 1])
    pos += 2
    if depth[u] < depth[v]:
        u, v = v, u
    diff = depth[u] - depth[v]
    for k in range(LOG):                     # lift the deeper vertex to the same depth
        if diff >> k & 1:
            u = up[k][u]
    if u != v:
        for k in range(LOG - 1, -1, -1):     # jump while the ancestors differ
            if up[k][u] != up[k][v]:
                u, v = up[k][u], up[k][v]
        u = up[0][u]
    out.append(u)
print("\n".join(map(str, out)))
